issues.legal_issue: Use of a common or descriptive mark on unrelated goods constitutes passing off when the mark has acquired a strong association with the plaintiff and the defendant dishonestly adopts it in a way likely to confuse consumers about the source.
material_facts: The respondent had built extraordinary goodwill and reputation in its mark through its newspaper and television businesses, and the mark was widely associated with the respondent in its principal market.
Although the mark was an ordinary word, it had acquired a secondary meaning identifying the respondent’s products and services.
The appellant used the mark for incense sticks, goods different from the respondent’s principal offerings, and used a similar artistic script, font and method of writing.
The Court found that the appellant’s adoption was dishonest and intended to benefit from the respondent’s reputation.

The Court found that the appellant’s use was likely to mislead consumers into believing that the incense sticks came from, or were associated with, the respondent, and would erode the respondent’s goodwill.
issues.conclusion: The appellant’s use of the mark on its incense sticks in the respondent’s principal market amounted to passing off, notwithstanding the difference between the parties’ businesses, and could not be permitted.
issues.legal_principle: A common or descriptive word may be protected in passing off when it has acquired a secondary meaning identifying a particular trader. Passing off requires goodwill, a misrepresentation that leads or is likely to lead the public to believe the defendant’s goods or services come from or are associated with the plaintiff, and resulting or likely damage. The parties need not operate in the same field where the circumstances establish likely source confusion and appropriation of goodwill. The Court relied on Reddaway & Co. v. Banham & Co., Reckitt & Colman Products Ltd. v. Borden Inc., Ruston & Hornsby Ltd. v. Zamindara Engineering Co., Laxmikant V. Patel v. Chetanbhai Shah, Satyam Infoway Ltd. v. Sifynet Solutions (P) Ltd., Mahendra & Mahendra Paper Mills Ltd. v. Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd., and the passing-off authorities concerning reputed marks discussed in the judgment.

rule.if: passing_off_proceeding and plaintiff_has_goodwill and mark_has_secondary_association and defendant_adopted_mark_dishonestly and likely_source_confusion and unrelated_goods

predicates.passing_off_proceeding: The plaintiff brought a claim alleging that the defendant’s use of a mark misrepresented the source or association of the defendant’s goods or services.
predicates.plaintiff_has_goodwill: The plaintiff had established goodwill and reputation in the relevant market through its goods, services or business.
predicates.mark_has_secondary_association: The public had come to associate the mark with the plaintiff, beyond the mark’s ordinary or descriptive meaning.
predicates.defendant_adopted_mark_dishonestly: The defendant adopted the mark intending to benefit from the plaintiff’s goodwill or reputation.
predicates.likely_source_confusion: The defendant’s use was likely to lead consumers to believe that the defendant’s goods or services came from, or were associated with, the plaintiff.
predicates.unrelated_goods: The defendant used the mark for goods or services different from those principally supplied by the plaintiff.

issues.definition: When a passing-off claim involves established goodwill, a mark associated with the plaintiff, dishonest adoption, likely source confusion and goods or services in a different field, the defendant’s use may be enjoined.
